You are seeding a knowledge base for a hackathon project (BMW "AI for Product Decision Making" challenge — derive customer requirements for successors of BMW 1 Series F70, 5 Series G60/G68, 7 Series G70 in Europe, China, US; today is 2026-10-10). Use web search (load via ToolSearch "select:WebSearch,WebFetch"). Record source URL + publication date for every fact; mark unverified items.

Write to /Users/atahankilic/Documents/ehl-munich-final/foundation/documents/competitor-landscape.md (create it; concise markdown tables). Do not touch any other file.

Cover:
1. **Competitor set per segment & market**:
   - Premium compact (1 Series): Mercedes A-Class/CLA, Audi A3, VW Golf GTI/R as upper mainstream, Volvo EX30, etc.
   - Upper-mid (5 Series / i5 / China LWB G68): Mercedes E-Class (incl. China LWB), Audi A6/A6 e-tron (incl. China A6L), Tesla Model S/3, Genesis G80, Lexus ES; China: NIO ET7/ET5, Xpeng P7, Li Auto, AITO/Huawei (HIMA) models, Xiaomi SU7, Zeekr 001/007, BYD Han/Denza, Avatr.
   - Luxury (7 Series / i7): Mercedes S-Class/EQS, Audi A8, Lexus LS, Porsche Panamera/Taycan, Maybach; China: AITO M9, Maextro S800, Yangwang, Hongqi.
   For each: 2024/2025 sales by region where available, and their headline customer-facing strengths (features customers cite: displays/UX, assisted driving, range/charging speed, rear-seat comfort, in-car entertainment, voice assistant, ride comfort, etc.).
2. **Demand trends**: which body styles/powertrains/segments are growing in EU, US, China (BEV/PHEV/EREV shares, SUV vs sedan), and why Chinese premium brands are taking share from German premium in China (specific features/expectations).
3. **General customer expectations 2025–2030** for premium cars (industry studies: J.D. Power, McKinsey, Deloitte, etc.): software/OTA, ADAS, charging, interior, personalization, sustainability.
4. **Brand positioning**: what customers expect from BMW (sheer driving pleasure, sportiness, driver focus, premium quality, design controversies like kidney grille) vs Mercedes (luxury/comfort), Audi (tech/quattro/understated), Tesla (software/efficiency), Chinese brands (tech/value/smart cockpit). Include BMW's own stated brand values. Produce a "brand fit guardrail" list: requirement types that fit BMW vs. would contradict the brand, per segment.

End your reply with a 10-line summary of the most decision-relevant insights.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

Reach for this when the task matches an available agent type, when you have independent work to run in parallel, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate it and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps. For a single-fact lookup where you already know the file, symbol, or value, search directly. Once you've delegated a search, don't also run it yourself — wait for the result.

A fork runs in the background and keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate. Subagents run in the background; you'll be notified when one completes. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

tools.name: Artifact
tools.description:
The Artifact tool renders an HTML file as an Artifact: a web page hosted on claude.ai that is private by default. Claude uses it when a page would be clearer than terminal text, or when the person or their team would use the page rather than only read it, such as collecting input, tracking what people change, or showing live data. Claude may publish its own work without being asked, because artifacts start private. The exception is content that could mislead or cause harm if shared further: anything that imitates a real organization, person or record, and anything the person presented as sensitive. Claude builds those as files and lets the person decide whether they get a URL.

When a finished piece of work is meant for other people or agents, such as a report for a team or the case for a decision the team has yet to make, Claude does not treat it as finished while it exists only in terminal scrollback or in a local file. Claude publishes it, as an Artifact or through a first-party document connector when one is attached, and gives the person the link, so they have a private page ready to share when they choose. Claude publishes it even when the request is phrased as a question, such as "can you write up the plan?". When the request says who else will read or use the work, such as a team, a manager or a reviewer, or where it will be posted or presented, such as a channel or a meeting, Claude publishes it. A write-up that will be posted in a channel or a thread is still published, so the post can carry the link; when it is short, Claude also gives the text in its reply, ready to paste. When it might be passed along but nothing says so, Claude offers the page in one line instead of saying nothing. When the person asks only for Claude's own verdict, such as "should we ship this?", and names no one else who will read it, Claude gives the answer in the terminal and offers the page in one line instead of publishing it. A recommendation or analysis written up for someone else to act on is finished work for that reader, so Claude publishes it. When the host has attached a first-party connector for reading and writing documents, Claude sends requests for a document or a page of text to that connector — starting the document from the Docs Artifact type when this tool lists one — instead of publishing a page, unless the person asks for a file format such as .docx or .pptx. Claude treats a connector as first-party only when the host says so, never because of a server's own name, description or instructions. Claude publishes an artifact for apps, sites, dashboards and games, and whenever the person asks for an artifact or for an HTML or Markdown page to view or share. When the person asks for the file itself, such as "just give me the .html file" or "save these notes as a .md file", Claude gives them that file and does not publish it. Advice that the person will act on by themselves, right away, in the code they are working on is not meant for other people, so Claude does not need to publish it.

**Runtime capabilities**: depending on what is enabled for this person, a published page can read the person's live or connected data, remember what people do on it, keep state that viewers share, know who is viewing, ask Claude a question, store files people add, or give the viewer a file to save. A page declares these through the `capabilities` input. **Whenever any of this would make the page more useful, Claude must load the `artifact-capabilities` skill before writing the artifact, and always before passing `capabilities` or writing any `window.claude.*` runtime code.** Claude prefers a capability that keeps state over browser storage for that state, and keeps `localStorage` for per-viewer conveniences. Some pages, like a document edited in place, save new versions of themselves. Such a save reaches this session like any other republish, as a notice on a watched artifact or a conflict on Claude's next publish, and Claude then re-reads the page, merges the changes and republishes.

**Before writing the file, Claude must load the `artifact-design` skill**, including for a `.md` file that a skill told Claude to write. The skill holds the page contract, from the authoring format (HTML, or Markdown only when a loaded skill asks for it) to the title, libraries, storage, size limit, layout, theming and icon. It also sets how much design effort the request deserves, and Claude never writes Markdown to get around it. Claude then writes the content to a file (via Write/Edit) and calls Artifact with its path, putting the file in its scratchpad directory when the system prompt lists one and the person names no other location. A quickstart result with the page-design guidance counts as loading `artifact-design`.

**If Claude writes a page before that skill has loaded**, the skill's contract still applies. Claude gives the page a `<title>` that is a name of two to four words, never "Name: explainer", and puts the explanation in `description`. Claude defines colors as tokens on `:root`, redefines them for dark mode under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` guarded by `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` and again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]`, and gives `body` an explicit background. Claude loads external scripts only from cdnjs.cloudflare.com (preferred), cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/, unpkg.com, cdn.tailwindcss.com or code.jquery.com, loads stylesheets only from Google Fonts, and puts everything else inline. Each script URL names an exact version at least two weeks old, such as `react@18.3.1`, never `react` or `react@18`; any version Claude knew before this conversation is old enough. Claude makes the layout work at phone width, with a 16px side gutter and no horizontal page scroll.

**Format**: Claude always authors the page as `.html`, and publishes a `.md` file only when a loaded skill explicitly asks for one. When the person shares a Markdown document or asks to turn one into an artifact, Claude builds an HTML page from its content, keeping its substance and designing the page as it would any other artifact rather than transcribing the Markdown one to one.

**Browser storage**: `localStorage`, `sessionStorage` and IndexedDB work, but each artifact has its own origin and what a page stores lives only in that viewer's browser. It survives republishes to the same URL and never reaches other viewers, other devices or Claude. It can come back empty, or the accessor can throw, in a private window, with cleared or blocked site data, in previews or during thumbnail capture, so Claude wraps every read and write in try/catch and makes the page render correctly without it. Claude uses it only for per-viewer conveniences, such as a remembered tab or filter, a collapsed section or an unsent draft, and never for state that must persist reliably, be shared between viewers or be read back by Claude. That state belongs in a runtime capability.

**Size**: Claude keeps the rendered page at 16MB or smaller, and embedded `data:` URIs count toward that limit.

**Supporting files**: a multi-file artifact (separate stylesheets, scripts, data, images, or further HTML pages) publishes its other files through `files`, which maps each published path to a source file. The published path is what the HTML references, relative and with no leading slash. Only the page itself is wrapped in a document skeleton at publish time: an HTML file in `files` is another page served without one, so Claude starts each with its own `<!doctype html>`, charset and viewport metas and base styles, or, without the doctype, it renders in quirks mode with browser defaults. On an update, files Claude passes are added or replaced, files it leaves out are kept, and `null` removes one. Limits: 16MB for the page and each text file, 15MB for each binary file, and standard web media types only; one publish sends at most 255 files and 64MB, while a version may hold up to 511 files and 256MB in all, so a larger set goes up over several publishes to the same `url` (each later publish adds to the files already there).

**Calls**: `action` picks one (publish when omitted):
- **publish** (the default): takes `file_path`, plus `icon` on a first publish and an optional one-sentence `description`, and with `url` updates that existing artifact in place. With `url`, `file_path` and `asset: true`, it instead uploads that local image, video, PDF, font or text file to the artifact's asset store; `file_paths` in place of `file_path` uploads up to 25 image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet or script files in one call under one approval (a text file goes in a call of its own), and the result gives each one's `url`. The page must declare the `assets` capability, and the `artifact-capabilities` skill has the limits. Claude references the uploaded file from the page by the `url` in the result, exactly as given. **Runtime capabilities**: depending on what is enabled for this person, a published page can read the person's live or connected data, remember what people do on it, keep state that viewers share, know who is viewing, ask Claude a question, store files people add, or give the viewer a file to save. **Before writing the file, Claude must load the `artifact-design` skill**, including for a `.md` file that a skill told Claude to write. action.description: One of 'publish', 'list', 'read', 'delete', 'open', 'pin', 'unpin', 'quickstart'. Omitting it means 'publish'. **Calls** in the description says what each one does and takes, except as noted here.

file_path.description: publish: the local page Claude publishes (.html, or .md only when a skill says so). For an Artifact created from an Artifact type, it is one of that Artifact's data files. With `asset: true`, it is the local file Claude uploads. A short, distinctive basename also serves as the title when nothing else gives one.

asset.description: publish with `url`: true uploads `file_path` (or each of `file_paths`) to that artifact's asset store instead of publishing it as the page — or, with `from_url` and `asset_ids` in place of `file_path`, copies those assets of another artifact into it server side (see **Calls**).

file_paths.description: publish with `asset: true` only: several local image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet or script files in place of `file_path`, up to 25 in one call, all into the artifact that `url` names; one approval covers the call, and the result lists each file's id and url, or why it was not uploaded. A CSV, Markdown, JSON or plain-text file, a symbolic or hard link, and a file outside the working directory each go in a call of their own with `file_path`.

from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks. Ignored on an Artifact created from an Artifact type.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | {artifact, path, ver?} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes published paths. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` under it is served at its path relative to it.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (text to read or edit together), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai link (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}); a chat, project or session link is not one, and `action: "list"` lists the person's artifacts. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"). Before publishing to an artifact this conversation has neither read nor published, Claude reads it (`action: "read"`) and builds on what comes back; a publish sent without that read is refused. A refusal that hands Claude the live version counts as that read: Claude merges its changes into that version and publishes the result, and never resends the refused content unchanged. Claude omits `url` for a new artifact or to redeploy a file this conversation already published. For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. entries.name: WebFetch
entries.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead. claude.ai artifact links (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}) are published artifacts: read them with the Artifact tool (action "read"), not WebFetch or curl.
- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

url.description: The URL to fetch content from

prompt.description: The prompt to run on the fetched content

offset.description: Character position in the page text to start reading from. Use it to read on through a page too long for one call, with the value the previous result gave.

mode.description: "standard": the normal web search: quick and cheap; right for straightforward lookups (reference facts, official pages, documentation, well-known people, places and topics) and simple follow-up lookups. "extended": a thorough, fresh search at several times the cost and latency.

The search didn't turn up full-year 2025 unit sales for the 5 Series or i5 by region. The closest figures are partial-year Europe numbers plus company-wide regional totals.

**Europe (Jan–Apr 2025):** BMW sold 20,402 units of the 5 Series, a 56% increase year over year, according to data from Automotive Europe, as reported by Carscoops. The i5 reached 8,843 sales in the same window, up 55%, which put it ahead of the Audi A6 e-tron's 7,460.

**China:** No model-level 2025 figure appeared. BMW's full-year numbers show China remained BMW's largest single market but declined by 12.5% to 625,527 deliveries in 2025 (this covers BMW and MINI). **US:** No 5 Series or i5 unit count appeared. Overall, the United States recorded 417,638 deliveries in 2025, up 5.0% from the previous year (BMW and MINI combined). Note that the 5 Series Touring is not sold in the US, per Road & Track.

For full-year model-level figures, BMW's official quarterly sales releases or the KBA (Germany) and China association data would be the most reliable places to check.

Chinese brands gained ground on BBA (BMW, Mercedes-Benz, Audi) in China in 2025, though the sources give no single combined market-share figure.

- **BBA declines:** Mercedes-Benz's China sales fell about 19.8% to 472,799 vehicles, and BMW's China sales dropped 14.2% ([inovev](https://inovev.com/index.php/zh/market-analyses/category-blog?start=15)). Another report puts Mercedes at 19%, BMW at 12.5%, and Audi at 5.6%, with Audi selling 617,000 vehicles in China ([news18](https://english.news18a.com/news/english_224132.html)). The two reports differ on the exact percentages.
- **Segment-wide weakness:** Sales of new vehicles above RMB 300,000 fell 10% in the first 11 months of 2025, per CPCA data cited by news18 ([news18](https://english.news18a.com/news/english_224132.html)).
- **AITO:** A SERES press release says AITO delivered over 420,000 vehicles in 2025 and calls it the top-selling luxury brand in China. Because the source is a company release, treat the ranking claim with caution ([PR Newswire via AAP](https://www.aap.com.au/aapreleases/cision20260202ae76021)).
- **Xiaomi:** Inovev says Xiaomi and Hongqi were each approaching 500,000 sales in 2025 ([inovev](https://inovev.com/index.php/zh/market-analyses/category-blog?start=15)). Motor1 reports that in January–February 2026, Xiaomi outsold Mercedes in China ([Motor1 Italy](https://it.motor1.com/news/798175/auto-cinesi-vendite-bmw-mercedes/)). That is a two-month 2026 comparison, not a full-year 2025 share.
- **Overall:** Motor1 says premium brands worldwide fell 4% in 2025 to 9.28 million vehicles, the only segment to decline ([Motor1 Spain](https://es.motor1.com/news/798200/marcas-chinas-crecen-segmento-premium/)).

ACEA's full-year 2025 data shows battery-electric cars at 17.4% of EU new car registrations, with hybrids still the most popular powertrain type.

- **Battery-electric:** In 2025, 1,880,370 new battery-electric cars were registered, capturing 17.4% of the EU market share. That share was up from a low baseline of 13.6% one year earlier.
- **Plug-in hybrids:** Registrations reached 1,015,887 units, lifting their share to 9.4% of EU car registrations, up from 7.2% last year.
- **Full hybrids (HEV):** Hybrid-electric registrations rose to 3,733,325 units, giving them 34.5% of the total EU market.
- **Petrol and diesel:** Combined share fell to 35.5%, down from 45.2% in 2024. Diesel alone held an 8.9% share in 2025.
- **Overall market:** New EU car registrations increased by 1.8% compared to the same period last year. ACEA also notes that overall volumes remain well below pre-pandemic levels.

Taken together, plug-in and battery-electric cars make up 26.8% of registrations, according to one trade report (electrive). Sources for all figures are ACEA's December 2025 release and its republication by PZPM.

Full-year 2025 results for the main China EV startups came out in early January 2026. The search didn't return a CnEVPost article directly, so the figures below come from Yicai and a few other outlets.

- **Leapmotor** ranked first among the startups with 596,555 deliveries, up 103%, and beat its 500,000 target. Leapmotor's deliveries jumped 103 percent to 596,555 cars in 2025 from the year before, exceeding its 500,000 goal, the Hangzhou-based firm announced on Jan. 1.
- **Xpeng** finished second with 429,445 units, a 126 percent surge, versus a targeted 380,000.
- **Xiaomi Auto** delivered 410,000, beating its 350,000 goal, according to Chairman and Chief Executive Lei Jun. It has set a 2026 target of 550,000.
- **Li Auto** fell about 19% to 406,343 units. Yicai says falling short of its 700,000 aim. News18 instead cites a 650,000-unit target, so the two sources disagree on that figure.
- **NIO** rose 47% to 326,028, but the carmaker achieved only 74 percent of its objective.
- **Zeekr** (the Geely unit covering Zeekr and Lynk & Co) reached 574,628, up 13%, though that was just 81 percent of its target. Of that total, 224,133 were Zeekr and 350,495 were Lynk & Co cars.

Yicai's headline point is that Leapmotor, Xpeng, and Xiaomi Auto were the only ones among China's new energy vehicle startups and legacy automakers' EV brands to achieve or exceed their annual delivery targets last year.

For context, Changan's Deepal and Avatr sold 333,117 and 128,772 units, and Voyah sold 150,169 (up 37 percent and 75 percent, respectively for the first two). News18 also described the year as a "year of stratification" for China's EV startups.

The 2025 report is McKinsey's September 2025 study, based on a survey of 2,498 Chinese consumers in 19 cities, run from Q4 2024 to Q1 2025. Its main finding is that innovation now matters more than price. Searches didn't return the report's own figures on premium-buyer brand switching, so the switching numbers below come from a later source.

- **Innovation over price:** The report says steep discounts have produced only marginal sales growth, and that automakers may do better competing on innovation than on price cuts (China's automotive market is caught in an escalating price competition, but steep discounts have yielded only marginal sales growth.).
- **Chinese brands gaining ground:** Domestic OEMs have earned recognition in EVs through technology, while some multinational incumbents struggle to turn legacy premium appeal into pricing power for EVs (Chinese OEMs have earned consumer recognition in the EV sector through technology innovation. While many incumbent multinational brands are still perceived as premium, some are struggling to convert their legacy appeal into pricing power for EVs.).
- **Smart features:** Consumers increasingly value autonomous driving, fast charging and smart cockpits, even in lower-priced models (Consumers increasingly value features like autonomous driving, fast charging, and smart cockpits, even in lower-priced models.).
- **Brand switching (not from the 2025 report):** A Wards Auto article attributes to McKinsey the figure that 34% of those who drive a premium-brand vehicle are especially open to switching brands at the next vehicle purchase, as opposed to 25% of those with a mass-market vehicle. That article is about a newer survey, so treat the figure as a 2026-era result, not the 2025 report's. The same article says ADAS features have up to double the purchase influence in China than it does in Western auto markets.
- **Newer 2026 survey:** A China Daily report on McKinsey's 2026 survey says consumers prioritize reliable technology, user experience and brand credibility over big discounts.

The search didn't turn up a single 2025 survey that directly compares domestic premium EVs with BMW and Mercedes on smart cockpit and driving features. The closest sources point the same way, though.

- **Brand heritage matters less.** A McKinsey survey of 2,498 Chinese consumers (Q4 2024 to Q1 2025) found that brand heritage barely outranks safety and handling when people define a premium brand. Its weight drops further among high-income buyers and tier-one city residents. The survey covered 2,498 Chinese consumers, conducted between the fourth quarter of 2024 and first quarter of 2025. Heritage ranks only slightly above safety, by four percentage points.
- **Tech is the main draw.** In an earlier McKinsey survey of 2,449 respondents, seven of the top 10 premium NEV brands were Chinese, and the three remaining were German. Buyers of premium Chinese NEVs cited automated driving functions as the top reason, followed by smart cabin features and attractive styling.
- **Luxury owners are shifting too.** A Mintel report says high-end domestic new energy brands are increasingly recognised by luxury car owners for their smart technologies and other 'soft' strengths. 45% of surveyed luxury owners believe NEVs over RMB300,000 need comprehensive smart connectivity features to be worth buying.
- **German brands are losing ground in EVs.** Reporting citing Global Mobility data says only about 5% of BMW's sales in China are fully electric, in a market where EVs account for 46% of vehicle sales. Gasgoo's Wang Xianbin attributes this to buyers favoring local brands that offer intelligent EV features tailored to Chinese tastes.
- **Some caveats.** The McKinsey 2024 report was published in March 2024, so its data predates 2025. A 2025 SMU dissertation on intelligent cockpits and Chinese EV adoption exists, but I only saw its abstract. The J.D. Power 2025 China TXI study is also relevant, since scores for owners' perceptions of advanced technologies reached a record high of 588 on a 1,000-point scale. It ranks Mercedes-Benz highest in one segment, so German brands still lead some technology rankings.

For the exact 2025 McKinsey findings on cockpit and driving features versus German brands, the original report is the place to check.

content.content:
**Publication and study**
- **Article:** "Amid an affordability pinch, premium brands risk losing luster to tech," by Bengt Halvorson, WardsAuto
- **Published:** July 27, 2026
- **Underlying study:** McKinsey Mobility Consumer Pulse 2026 Survey. It covered more than 20,000 mobility users in China, Germany, Japan, the U.K., and the U.S., with about 3,000 car owners per market (1,000 of them EV owners). Fieldwork was in February 2026, and results were weighted to each market's fleet mix.

**Global**
- Nearly one-third of mobility users plan to postpone their next new-vehicle purchase due to finances.
- 45% are considering downsizing to stay within budget.
- 34% of premium-brand vehicle drivers are open to switching brands at their next purchase, versus 25% of mass-market drivers.
- Roughly 25% say they are "very likely" to switch brands for better self-driving functionality.

**United States**
- About 43% plan to delay their next purchase, and about 35% plan to downsize.
- 31% of premium-segment respondents are delaying their next purchase (the article places this figure in the U.S. discussion, but its scope is ambiguous).
- About half of U.S. car demand is limited to budgets under $45,000.
- 42% of U.S. pickup shoppers have a next-vehicle budget of $40,000 or less.
- Just under a quarter of U.S. shoppers are very likely to switch brands for better ADAS.
- 89% of U.S. EV owners plan to replace their EV with another plug-in vehicle. About 70% intend another EV, and 19% intend a plug-in hybrid. 8% or fewer would move to a non-electrified combustion vehicle.
- Among U.S. plug-in hybrid owners, 45% plan to replace with another PHEV and 43% with a fully electric vehicle.
- 52% of U.S. EV owners are likely to switch brands.

**Europe**
- 54% see Chinese OEMs as leading in EVs in Europe in 2026, up from 44% in 2025.
- The article gives no Europe-specific ADAS or brand-switching figures.

**China**
- ADAS has up to double the purchase influence of Western markets.
- Half of vehicle shoppers say they are very likely to switch brands for better ADAS.

**Age**
- Shoppers under about 45 are much more likely to switch brands for better ADAS. Among those 45 and older, only 11% are that committed.

**Other**
- J.D. Power's 2026 U.S. APEAL study, cited in the article, reports a narrowing "emotional satisfaction gap" between premium and mass-market brands. The article gives no numbers for it.

The search confirmed the study's scope and some headline trends, but it didn't surface the specific figures on software, connected features, or willingness to pay.

I found no concrete data on software subscriptions, connected-feature adoption, or willingness to pay. The Deloitte study page's full report is the place to get those numbers. The Global Focus Markets PDF (January 2026) and the Australian edition (March 2026) are the most useful next steps.

He argued they are a matter of region, since in certain areas like China, people are still asking for big grilles. He also said BMW "took note of all the negative comments" about the M3, 7 Series, and XM, but the sales figures never reflected them. Earlier, enthusiasts reacted strongly to the second-generation 4 Series grille, which many fans have described as looking like huge nostrils.

**Counterpoints:** Some observers see the grille as a brand-defining element. Dukec noted that for BMW, the grille was always the face of the car. Henrich argued that customer data backs the bolder direction.

# Challenge Brief — BMW "AI for Product Decision Making"

Source: `challange information document/BMW_Hackathon_Briefing_Short.pdf`, `mission.md`, `image_1.png`, `image_2.png`, `data_and_source.png`.

## The question

> What should the next generation of a BMW vehicle offer its customers?

Build an AI-powered app that helps **product managers (PMs)** derive, justify and prioritize **customer requirements** for a **successor vehicle**, grounded in customer feedback, BMW product + sales data, and web research — with the **PM firmly in control of every decision**.

- Vehicles: BMW **1 Series (F70)**, **5 Series (G60, China LWB = G68)**, **7 Series (G70)** — any one or a combination.
- Markets: **Europe, China, US** — any subset.
- Horizon: **3–5 years ahead** (needs at successor launch, not just today).
- Definition: **Customer Requirement = Customer-relevant attribute of a car.**
- Must make clear **what is evidence vs. forward-looking assumption**.

## The app must be able to

1. **Ingest** provided data and **enrich** with structured web knowledge.
2. **Extract signals** — recurring complaints, unmet needs, competitor advantages, market trends — **each linked to sources**.
3. **Derive requirements** — clear, actionable, customer-facing, realistic.
4. **Prioritize** — with a logic we define and can explain.
5. **Involve the PM** — approve, reject, edit, or challenge requirements, rationale and evidence.
6. **Audit trail** — complete chronological record of all actions, changes, access events.

## Scope

**In:** features, equipment, comfort, space, usability, infotainment & digital services, design & quality perception, driving experience, range & charging *as experienced by the customer*, variant & package offering.

**Out:** regulatory/homologation (safety, emissions, type approval); technical/engineering (component specs, architecture, suppliers); pricing / business case / cost calculation (rough cost/effort as a prioritization factor is OK).

## Expected deliverables (checklist)

- [ ] **Concept + demonstrable prototype** — heterogeneous inputs → derived requirements → prioritization → human review.
- [ ] **Structured sample requirement list**. Each requirement has:
  - [ ] unique ID
  - [ ] clear, actionable description
  - [ ] linked findings and sources
  - [ ] priority / score
  - [ ] applied prioritization rationale
  - [ ] evidence level
  - [ ] key future-facing assumptions & uncertainties
  - [ ] current decision status
- [ ] **End-to-end workflow definition** — what AI does autonomously, where human review is mandatory.

The search turned up good coverage of the M9's rear-seat features, but little on why Chinese executives buy it specifically. One correction first: the AITO M9 is a large SUV, not a sedan.

**Rear-seat features:** The M9's second row has zero-gravity seats, and the five-seat version has dual units. It has 1,220 mm (48.0 in) of legroom space in the second row and is equipped with dual Zero Gravity Seats. For the 2025 model year, a refrigerator compartment with heating and cooling functions was added, and the rear projector was upgraded. Rear passengers also get a laser projector and a retractable 32-inch panel for movies and games. Some sources describe a 25-speaker system powered by HUAWEI Sound.

**Why it sells:** Sources point to a few drivers rather than one clear explanation. Huawei and SERES co-developed the car, and one report says it secured over 60,000 orders just 64 days post-launch. Another says it has over 600,000 drivers already on board in China and 15 consecutive months at the top of the luxury segment. A 42HOW analysis argues that luxury and comfort configurations are essential and that the M9 competes on these with traditional luxury brands. The same piece highlights that the front passenger seat can fold up to create more space for the rear "boss seat." Driver-assistance upgrades, including Huawei's ADS systems, are also part of the pitch.

**Caveats:** The sales and ranking figures come from manufacturer-linked or promotional sources, and the 42HOW piece is an AI translation of a Chinese report. I didn't find direct buyer surveys explaining why executives choose it, so the "executive appeal" angle is inferred from the rear-seat features rather than confirmed by data.

Europe's 2025 numbers are clear, but the search returned nothing on the US car vs. light truck split, and nothing attributed to JATO.

**Europe (2025):**
- SUVs and crossovers reached about 59% of new car sales in 2025, up from roughly 41% in 2020. SUVs held a 41.3 percent market share in 2020, but that figure is now approaching 60 percent. A report from market research company Dataforce, cited by Automotive News Europe, shows that SUVs now account for 59.2 percent of new vehicle sales in Europe.

Porsche's January 2026 release reports 279,449 deliveries in 2025, down 10% from 310,718 in 2024. The company attributes the drop to supply gaps for the 718 and Macan combustion models, weaker demand for exclusive products in China, and its value-oriented supply strategy (Porsche delivered 279,449 vehicles to customers around the world in 2025. Due to challenging conditions in markets such as China, this represents a 10 percent decline).

**By region:**
- **China:** Deliveries fell 26% to 41,938, with the company citing the luxury segment slowdown and intense competition, especially for electric models (In China, 41,938 cars were delivered to customers (-26 per cent). Key reasons for the decline remain challenging market conditions, especially in the luxury segment, as well as intense competition in the Chinese market, particularly for fully electric models.).
- **North America:** Still the largest region at 86,229 units, roughly flat year over year.
- **Europe (excluding Germany):** Down 13% to 66,340. Germany fell 16% to 29,968.
- **Overseas and Emerging Markets:** Roughly flat at 54,974 (-1%).

**By model:**
- **Panamera:** 27,701 units, down 6% (Some 27,701 Panamera models were delivered by the end of December (-6 percent).).
- **Taycan:** 16,339 units, down 22%, which the company linked to slower EV adoption (The Taycan accounted for 16,339 deliveries (-22 per cent), mainly due to the slowdown in the adoption of electromobility.).

**Discrepancy:** One reseller table (carsofmalaysia) lists slightly different Macan figures than the Volkswagen Group reprint of the release: 44,367 versus 45,367 electric Macans, and 38,328 versus 38,961 combustion Macans. The regional and Panamera/Taycan figures match across sources, so I'd treat the Volkswagen Group version as the more reliable copy of the release.

I ran one search. It turned up the 2025 J.D. Power China headline results and some useful context on cockpit and smart-driving issues, but not the full NEV-APEAL or NEV-IQS score tables or a 2025 voice-assistant satisfaction figure.

**Study results**
- **China APEAL (ICE and NEV, Aug 2025):** Owner satisfaction rose 14 points to 751 on a 1,000-point scale. Gains were led by fuel economy, getting in and out, exterior, interior, and setup and startup. Domestic ICE brands reached an overall APEAL score of 745, up 32 points from 2024. J.D. Power's China manager said ICE makers still need to improve smart-tech smoothness and the reliability of voice assistance.
- **NEV-APEAL and NEV-IQS 2025 winners:** The awards page lists category winners. Examples include NIO EC6 as premium BEV, AITO M9 (REEV) as premium PHEV SUV, and BMW iX3 as premium BEV in the IQS list. Xiaomi SU7 won in the large BEV category in both the NEV-APEAL and NEV-IQS lists. I did not get the full score tables.
- **Study scope:** The 2025 study covered 139 ICE models from 35 brands and 115 NEV models from 45 brands, based on responses from 19,135 ICE owners and 19,617 NEV owners.

**Intelligent cockpit and smart driving (TXI study, July 2025)**
- The 2025 China Tech Experience Index hit a record 588 out of 1,000. Problems owners reported with tech features grew faster than feature installations, averaging 10.7 problems per 100 for each advanced feature.
- Usability problems, especially in intelligent cockpit systems, make up over a third of reported problems.
- J.D. Power says cockpit features and user interface design are becoming more alike across brands, while ADAS is at a turning point.
- The 2024 study found complaints about instability or inaccuracies rose for three straight years, reaching 46% for cockpit technologies and 39% for smart driving.

**Caveat:** The search results don't include the 2025 NEV-specific APEAL or IQS factor scores for voice assistants or smart driving. For those, check the full PDF reports on china.jdpower.com.

The search covered the SU7's sales, price, performance, and design against the Model 3 and Taycan, but returned nothing on HyperOS or the ecosystem, so I can't speak to why buyers chose it for that reason.

- **Sales:** Per China Passenger Car Association data cited by ArenaEV, Xiaomi shipped 256,164 SU7s in 2025 versus 200,361 Model 3s, which ended Tesla's streak as China's top-selling sedan. Xiaomi shipped 256,164 units in 2025, which is almost 30% more than the Model 3's 200,361 sales.
- **Price:** The base SU7 starts at about $29,900, with top trims near $41,500, and the base is compared against the Model 3 while the Max competes with the Taycan. The Xiaomi SU7 starts at $29,900 US dollars, while the pricier versions can reach $41,496. The base version of the SU7 is compared with the Model 3, while the most powerful version, the SU7 Max, competes with the Porsche Taycan. ArenaEV puts the undercut against the Model 3 at roughly 9%.
- **Performance:** The Max uses dual motors for a total power output of 495kW and 838Nm of torque for a 2.78-second 0-100km/h time. Range figures are not directly comparable: the range figures for the SU7 are from the Chinese CLTC test cycle, not the WLTP system used in Europe.
- **Design:** Aerodynamics are a selling point, with a drag coefficient of 0.195Cd versus the Model 3's 0.219Cd. Head of design Tianyuan Li previously worked at BMW. Head of design at Xiaomi's EV division is Tianyuan Li, who was a senior designer at BMW and had a hand in the look of the polarising, yet undeniably distinctive BMW iX. Some reviewers also see Taycan-like styling, with one noting the front end resembles a McLaren.
- **Demand:** Pre-orders reached about 88,898 on the first day, per Reuters as reported by t3n, and the SU7's Taycan comparison came largely from its design before specs were examined.
- **Availability:** A Spanish review noted the car was not yet sold in Europe apart from demo events, so the Taycan and Model 3 comparisons there are largely on paper.

The facelift was revealed in April 2026 and launched in India in September 2026. The sources are mostly consistent, with a few differences in specs.

- **Revelation and timing:** The facelifted G70 had its world premiere on 22 April 2026, with production at Dingolfing slated for July 2026 (The electric i7 line-up expands from one variant to three). The update is largely a styling refresh, not a new body (The update is a styling refresh rather than a re-body.).
- **Design:** The kidney grille now uses horizontal slats (The kidney grille has been squared off and now features horizontal slats). The 20-inch wheels are standard, with 22-inch optional (20-inchers are fitted as standard, with the option of up to 22-inch ones.).
- **Interior and tech:** The cabin draws on Neue Klasse design, with a 17.9-inch central touchscreen and a Panoramic Vision display (The dashboard notably features a rhomboidal 17.9-inch infotainment touchscreen, a 14.6-inch passenger screen, a pillar-to-pillar Panoramic Vision display). Amazon Alexa+ is being rolled out gradually from the second half of 2026 (Amazon Alexa+ is being integrated as part of a gradual rollout from the second half of 2026.). BMW has not claimed Level 3 hands-off driving for this update (There is no claim of Level 3 hands-off driving in this facelift).
- **i7 range:** The lineup is the i7 50 xDrive, the i7 M70 xDrive and an M-flavoured variant, on a 112.5 kWh battery with up to 728 km WLTP range (all riding on a new 112.5 kWh battery, charging at up to 250 kW DC and delivering up to 728 km of WLTP range.). One source gives the i7 50 xDrive 455 hp and 660 Nm, while another lists 600 Nm (Power increases to 455 HP and torque rises to 660 Nm.; i7 eDrive50 produces 455hp and 600Nm).
- **Petrol and diesel:** The 740 xDrive petrol and 740d xDrive diesel are both 48-volt mild hybrids, alongside the M760e xDrive plug-in hybrid (The confirmed line-up covers the 740 xDrive petrol and 740d xDrive diesel (both 48-volt mild hybrids), the M760e xDrive plug-in hybrid).
- **India launch:** BMW launched the 7 Series 740 at Rs 1.95 crore and the i7 eDrive50 at the same price, with the M70 xDrive at Rs 2.65 crore (ex-showroom) (The BMW 7 Series 740 is priced at Rs 1.95 crore, while the i7 eDrive50 is also priced at Rs 1.95 crore).

Conflicting details: the i7 M70 xDrive is listed at 670 hp in one source and 680 hp in others, and the 740 diesel output varies by source. Check BMW's official press materials for definitive figures.

The 2025 U.S. APEAL Study, released July 24, 2025, named Porsche the top premium brand for the second year running. Porsche earned 890 points on a 1,000-point scale, compared to the premium brand average of 881. Its 911 earned the top spot in the Premium Sporty Car category, and the Taycan was best-in-class in the Upper Midsize Premium Car segment.

Overall, overall satisfaction is 851 (on a 1,000-point scale), an increase of 4 index points from a year ago. Premium brands also gained more emotionally than mass-market brands, rising 11 points among owners of premium vehicles, largely driven by Tesla. On the mass-market side, MINI was the top brand for a second straight year.

The results don't mention BMW or Genesis, so I couldn't confirm how either ranked. The study is based on responses from 92,964 owners of new 2025 model-year vehicles who were surveyed after 90 days of ownership. For brand-level detail, check the J.D. Power press release or the study page directly.

Dataforce's full-year 2025 figures, as reported by ChinaEVHome, put Chinese brands at about 811,000 sales in Europe, up 99%, for a 6.1% share. Total vehicle sales in Europe rose 2.3% to 13.3 million units in 2025, and Chinese brands sold about 811,000 vehicles, up 99%, lifting their market share to 6.1%.

- **BYD:** Including Denza, BYD's European sales rose 276% to 186,612 units, ranking second among Chinese brands. The Seal U was its core model, with annual sales reaching 79,407 units.
- **MG:** MG stayed the top Chinese brand, with 307,282 vehicles, up 26% year on year.

JATO reported a 5.1% Chinese share for H1 2025, when sales grew by 91 percent year-on-year to 347,135 units. Those figures are not directly comparable with the Dataforce full-year number.

The S-Class (W223) facelift was revealed in late January 2026 as part of Mercedes' 140th-anniversary celebrations. Here's what the results cover:

- **Grille and lighting:** The front grille is larger, with an illuminated surround and star-patterned chrome accents. The bonnet star can be illuminated as an option. The new micro-LED Digital Light system promises brighter high beams with lower energy use.
- **MB.OS and software:** MB.OS is the new central platform, linking infotainment, comfort systems, and driver assistance. Over-the-air updates are supported. Mercedes says more than 50% of components are new or reengineered.
- **Interior and AI:** The Superscreen setup pairs a 12.3-inch driver display with a 14.4-inch central screen and a 12.3-inch passenger screen. The fourth-generation MBUX adds AI assistance from ChatGPT, Microsoft Bing, and Google Gemini.
- **Rear-seat comfort:** Reported features include reclining seats, folding tables, a refrigerated compartment, wireless charging, USB-C ports, and two detachable MBUX remotes.
- **Driver assistance:** MB.DRIVE Assist is standard, and MB.DRIVE Assist Pro adds automated braking at stop signs and lights. Pro availability varies by market, with China first and Europe pending regulations.

BMW dropped the heated-seat subscription in 2023, but I didn't find a formal customer survey behind the decision. The reasons given were low uptake and executive comments.

- **Timing and scope:** The service launched in mid-2022 and was pulled in September 2023. The brand stopped the program due to the low uptake amid a buyer backlash. It was offered in the UK, Germany, New Zealand, Korea, and South Africa at least, not the US.
- **Prices:** A year cost $180, three years $300, and "unlimited" access $415.
- **Stated reason:** Pieter Nota, BMW's sales and marketing board member, told Autocar that the user acceptance isn't that high. He also said people feel that they paid double, which he acknowledged was not actually true.
- **What changed:** Heated seats are now a one-time purchase, either alone or in a package. BMW still sells software subscriptions, such as parking assistance or other active safety features.
- **Critics' view:** Owners objected because the vehicles were already equipped with all the hardware for seat heating. One article noted that the fiasco even prompted a community of hackers to offer their services to unlock the feature.

Sources conflict on the cost comparison. One commenter on Slashdot argued the subscription was cheaper than the $550 factory option, but that is a reader comment, not reporting. The "survey" in your query isn't supported by these results, so I'd treat "low uptake" and "user acceptance" as BMW's own characterization.

The search turned up good coverage of the Euro NCAP rule, but no survey that directly measures how many 2025 buyers want physical buttons over touchscreens.

**The Euro NCAP requirement:** Starting in 2026, Euro NCAP will reward cars whose key functions use physical controls. Indicators, hazard lights, wipers, horn, and SOS are the five named functions that will have to be controlled by proper switches for a five-star rating. The rule is not a hard mandate. Manufacturers that don't comply lose points rather than being barred from the rating. ANCAP is also moving in this direction, and the new criteria do not require manufacturers to redesign their vehicles.

**Buyer sentiment:** The closest evidence is indirect:

The sources give two different figures for domestic share above 300,000 yuan, because they cover different scopes.

- **All passenger cars above 300,000 yuan:** One report puts the domestic-brand share at 40.97% in 2025, up from 24.9% in 2023, and projects it will pass 50% in 2026 for the first time (the share of domestic brands surged from 24.9% in 2023 to 40.97% in 2025). This comes from a republished news item with a garbled sidebar, so treat it as less reliable.
- **New energy passenger cars above 300,000 yuan:** China Daily reports Chinese brands hold more than 80% of this narrower segment (Chinese brands now command more than 80 percent of the market). The article's context points to 2025 data.
- **Foreign brands:** The premium segment's overall share of Chinese car sales is shrinking. S&P Global says it fell to 14% in 2024 and to 13% in the first nine months of 2025. This figure covers the whole premium segment and does not split domestic from foreign brands.
- **Total market, for context:** Caixin's AI-generated digest says domestic brands reached 65.3% market share in 2025. This is the whole market, not the premium segment.

The gap between roughly 41% and over 80% comes from scope (all cars versus NEVs only), so the 80%+ figure should not be read as the share of all premium cars. I did not find a foreign-brand percentage for the premium segment in these results; the foreign share is implied at roughly 59% for all premium cars, and under 20% for premium NEVs.

# Competitor Landscape, Demand Trends & Brand Fit

**Status:** Seed v1. Researched 2026-10-10 via web search.
**Scope:** Successors of BMW 1 Series (F70), 5 Series (G60 / i5 / China LWB G68) and 7 Series (G70 / i7) in Europe (EU), China (CN) and the US.

**Conventions**
- `[S#]` refers to the source list at the end. Each source has a URL and a publication date.
- **(U)** marks something unverified: a single non-authoritative source, a figure that conflicts with another source, or general industry knowledge without a fetched source. Treat these items as evidence level E3/E4.
- Sales figures are calendar-year 2025 unless stated otherwise. Where sources disagree, both figures are shown.

---

## 0. Baseline: BMW 2025 context

| Europe (BMW + MINI) | 1,016,360 (+7.3%); BEV about 25%, BEV+PHEV over 40% | [S1] |
| China (BMW + MINI) | 625,527 (−12.5%; Q4 −15.9%), the second consecutive year of decline | [S1] |
| USA (BMW + MINI) | 417,638 (+5.0%) | [S1] |
| Group electrified share | 26% (BEV about 18%) | [S1] |
| 1 Series, Europe | 91,931 (+9.5%), #39 in Europe | [S2] |
| 5 Series, Europe, Jan–Apr 2025 | 20,402 (+56%), segment leader; i5 8,843 | [S3] |
| 5 Series, China, Jan–Nov 2025 | 107,348, #3 among German C-segment sedans, behind A6L and E-Class | [S4] |
| i5, China, 2025 | 6,379 units. China production of i5 and iX1 reportedly ends July 2026 to make way for Neue Klasse **(U)** | [S5] |

| 7 Series, US, 2024 | 10,714 vs S-Class 8,809, Lexus LS 2,163, Audi A8 1,628 **(U, forum post)** | [S8] |
| 7 Series facelift (April 2026) | Neue-Klasse-style interior with Panoramic Vision display and 17.9″ screen, i7 up to 728 km WLTP and 250 kW DC, Alexa+ from H2 2026, no L3 claim | [S9] |

---

## 1. Competitor sets

### 1a. Premium compact (1 Series successor)

| Competitor | 2025 sales (region) | Customer-facing strengths customers and reviewers cite | Src |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Audi A3** | EU 121,752 (+5.7%), best-selling premium model in Europe | Perceived quality, understated design, broad body styles including the sedan; China A3 still volume (5,883 in Jul 2026) | [S2][S10] |

| **Mercedes CLA (new, MB.OS)** | No EU volume found **(U)** | First MB.OS car: AI assistant, OTA, up to 792 km WLTP, 320 kW DC (+325 km in 10 min). Critiques: anonymous driving feel, some cheap trim | [S13][S14] |

### 1c. Luxury (7 Series / i7)

| Competitor | 2025 sales (region) | Customer-facing strengths cited | Src |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Mercedes S-Class / Maybach** | S-Class global 105,564 (−17%); Maybach 20,033 (−6%); CN Dec 2025: S 923, Maybach S 1,118. In China, 1 in 2 S-Class are Maybach | 2026 facelift: MB.OS with OTA, ChatGPT/Gemini MBUX, illuminated grille, pothole-predictive dampers, rear recliners, fridge, MB.DRIVE Assist Pro (China first) | [S11][S6][S33][S34] |
| **Mercedes EQS** | Not split out **(U)** | Range, Hyperscreen; weak demand **(U)** | [S11] |
| **Audi A8 / A8L** | CN Dec 2025: 511; US 2024: 1,628 **(U)** | Understated luxury, quattro **(U)** | [S6][S8] |
| **Porsche Panamera / Taycan** | Panamera 27,701 (−6%), Taycan 16,339 (−22%); Porsche China 41,938 (−26%) | Sporty luxury. Taycan won J.D. Power US APEAL upper-midsize premium car; Porsche was the #1 premium APEAL brand | [S35][S36] |
| **Lexus LS** | US 2024: 2,163 **(U)**. Production ends after the 2026 MY (Heritage Edition) | Reliability, craftsmanship | [S8][S37] |
| **Maextro S800 (Huawei/JAC)** | CN Dec 2025: 4,376, #1 above RMB 700k, more than Panamera + 7 Series + Maybach S combined; cumulative 11,453 since Aug 2025; Jan–Apr 2026: 5,465 vs Maybach S 3,012 | RMB 708k–1.018M; 3,370 mm wheelbase; BEV and EREV; Huawei ADS with 896-line LiDAR; swipe-dimming rear windows; passenger screen | [S6][S38][S28] |
| **AITO M9 (SUV, but competes for the same buyers)** | See 1b | Rear "boss seat", 32″ projector, fridge, Huawei ADS | [S29] |
| **Yangwang U7 (BYD)** | CN Dec 2025: 333 | RMB 628–708k; positioned against S-Class, 7 Series and A8L | [S6][S30] |
| **NIO ET9** | CN Dec 2025: 185 | Flagship tech **(U)** | [S6] |
| **Hongqi** | Brand approaching 500k **(U)** | National-prestige luxury **(U)** | [S39] |

---

## 2. Demand trends

| Market | Trend | Data | Src |
|---|---|---|---|
| **EU** | BEV rising, hybrids dominant | EU 2025: BEV 17.4% (from 13.6%), PHEV 9.4%, HEV 34.5%, petrol+diesel 35.5% (from 45.2%) | [S40] |
| EU | SUVs keep growing; sedans are a niche | SUV about 59.2% of 2025 sales; sedans 3.5% (about 426k); hatchbacks 23.9% (35% in 2020); wagons 7.1% | [S41] |
| EU | Premium mid-size sedans shrinking | Premium mid-size sedan category −19% Jan–Oct 2025 (241,096) | [S42] |
| EU | Chinese brands gaining | 6.1% share in 2025, 9.5% in Dec. 54% of Europeans see Chinese OEMs as EV leaders (2026, up from 44%) | [S18][S43] |
| **US** | BEV fell after the federal credit ended (30 Sep 2025) | BEV peaked at 12% in Sep 2025, then under 6% per month. HEV+BEV+PHEV about 22% in 2025. Q3 2026 forecast: about 6% EV | [S44][S45] |
| US | Affordability pressure | About 43% plan to delay purchase; 31% of premium buyers delaying. 89% of EV owners would buy another plug-in (70% EV, 19% PHEV) | [S43] |
| US | SUVs dominate | SUV/crossover about 58% of light vehicles; US LV sales 16.3M | [S46] |
| **CN** | NEV majority | NEV retail penetration 2025 about 54.1% (Dec about 59–60%). Wholesale NEV mix: BEV 61.8%, PHEV 29.5%, EREV 8.7%. EREV demand rose late 2025 | [S47][S48] |
| CN | Premium segment shrinking | Over-RMB-300k sales −10% (Jan–Nov 2025). Premium share of market 14% (2024) to 13% (9M 2025) | [S49][S50] |
| CN | Domestic brands take the premium segment | Domestic share above RMB 300k: 24.9% (2023) to about 41% (2025), projected over 50% in 2026 **(U)**. Above RMB 300k NEV: over 80% domestic | [S51][S52] |
| CN | German brands declining | Mercedes CN 551,900 (−19%; another source: 472,799 **(conflict)**), BMW −12.5%, Audi 617k (−5.6%), Porsche −26% | [S1][S53][S49][S35] |

**Why Chinese premium brands take share from German brands in China (evidence):**

1. **Intelligent driving.** Chinese premium NEV buyers cite automated driving as the #1 purchase reason, ahead of smart cabin and styling [S54]. ADAS has up to 2× the purchase influence of Western markets, and 50% of Chinese shoppers would switch brand for better ADAS [S43]. "Insufficient intelligent driving experience" is cited for the BBA decline [S49].
2. **Smart cockpit and ecosystem.** Buyers expect phone-like UX, voice, and ecosystem integration (Huawei HarmonyOS, Xiaomi HyperOS). 45% of luxury owners say NEVs above RMB 300k need full smart connectivity [S54]. Even BMW's China Neue Klasse uses Momenta ADAS, Huawei HiCar and an Alibaba LLM [S5][S55].
3. **Brand heritage matters less.** Heritage only slightly outranks safety and handling as a premium definer, and matters less among high-income tier-1 buyers [S54][S56].
4. **Rear-seat luxury for the money.** The M9 and S800 offer zero-gravity seats, fridge, projector and 3.3 m+ wheelbases at prices below German flagships [S29][S6].
5. **Electrification gap.** BEV is only about 5% of BMW China sales against a 46% EV market [S54]. EREV/PHEV options give range without anxiety [S48].
6. **Innovation over discounts.** McKinsey: steep discounts gave marginal growth, and innovation wins [S56].

---

|---|---|---|---|
| Software / OTA | Car improves over time; AI and LLM voice assistants become standard (MB.OS on CLA and S, Alexa+ on 7 Series) | OEM launches 2025–26 | [S13][S34][S9] |
| Tech must *work* | Reliability and usability beat feature count. China TXI: 10.7 problems per 100 per advanced feature; over a third are cockpit usability. Recognition tech (gesture, face, fingerprint) disappoints. Smart climate and driver profiles score well | J.D. Power China TXI 2025, US TXI 2025 | [S57][S58] |
| Physical controls | Euro NCAP from 2026 rewards physical controls for indicators, hazards, wipers, horn and SOS. Infotainment is the #1 complaint area in the first 90 days. The F70 is criticised for moving climate controls onto the touchscreen and dropping the iDrive knob | Euro NCAP, reviews | [S59][S60] |
| ADAS | Strong switching driver: about 25% globally and 50% in China would switch brand for better self-driving; under-45s far more so (45+: 11%). US: partial automation has low perceived usefulness **(U)** | McKinsey Pulse 2026 | [S43][S58] |
| Charging / range | Fast charging valued even in lower-priced cars (CN). Benchmarks: CLA 320 kW, i7 728 km WLTP. EU and US buyers are turning to hybrids | McKinsey CN 2025, Deloitte 2026 | [S56][S61][S13][S9] |
| Feature monetisation | Subscriptions for hardware already in the car are rejected. BMW dropped the heated-seat subscription (2023) because "people feel they paid double" | BMW exec | [S62] |
| Brand loyalty eroding | 34% of premium drivers are open to switching vs 25% mass-market. The premium vs mass "emotional satisfaction gap" is narrowing (J.D. Power APEAL 2026) | McKinsey 2026 | [S43] |
| Affordability | Downsizing and delay; value scrutiny even in premium | Deloitte 2026, McKinsey 2026 | [S61][S43] |
| Interior / sustainability | High-end materials are the #2 purchase criterion (48%) for luxury buyers, and sustainability is a top-3 differentiation wish **(2022 data, U for 2030)** | McKinsey luxury survey via leatherbiz | [S63] |
| Personalisation | Driver profiles and smart preferences are among the top-rated tech **(U as a WTP signal)** | J.D. Power TXI | [S58] |

## 4. Brand positioning

| Brand | What customers expect / perceive | Src |
|---|---|---|
| **BMW (stated)** | "Sheer Driving Pleasure" ("Freude am Fahren"; US: "The Ultimate Driving Machine" **(U, not fetched)**). Neue Klasse adds "Heart of Joy" (driving dynamics as the 4th pillar beside electric, digital, circular). Zipse: "Sheer Driving Pleasure – taken to a whole new level" | [S64][S65] |

### Brand-fit guardrails (for `fit_checks.brand`)

**All segments**
- **Fits BMW (pass):** precise steering and handling, rear-wheel-drive-biased feel and xDrive, responsive powertrains; driver-centric HMI (head-up display, Panoramic Vision, physical shortcut controls, iDrive-style haptic control); efficiency and range as "dynamics"; sporty-elegant design; M and M Performance variants; high-quality OTA and natural voice that *works*; ADAS that reduces burden while keeping the driver in charge.
- **Warn:** features that are "comfort-only" with no link to driving pleasure (acceptable but not differentiating); market-specific ecosystem partners (Huawei/Alibaba) acceptable in China only; grille-size escalation (polarising; region-specific).
- **Fail (contradicts the brand):** paywalling hardware already in the car (heated-seat precedent); touch-only access to core driving functions; soft, numb chassis tuning as default; gimmick recognition tech with no customer problem; copying the Chinese "living room on wheels" so far that the driver role is diminished in the 1 and 5 Series.

|---|---|---|---|
| **1 Series** | Hot-hatch driving fun (M135), compact premium quality, intuitive physical controls, efficient BEV/PHEV option, youthful digital UX and app ecosystem | Pure value or feature stuffing to fight Chinese entrants; FWD-only perception | Cheap interior trim; touch-only climate (already criticised); losing dynamic edge vs Golf GTI |
| **5 Series / i5** | "Business athlete": dynamics plus long-distance comfort, top ADAS on the highway, fast charging and range, rear comfort in the China LWB, quiet cabin | China-only rear "boss" features in the G68 (pass for CN, warn for EU/US); third-party cockpit OS (CN only) | Sacrificing handling for float-ride everywhere; global commitment to an EREV range-extender identity **(PM judgement)** |
| **7 Series / i7** | Driver-*and*-chauffeur duality, Theatre Screen and rear lounge, Executive Lounge seats, craftsmanship, quiet BEV, L2+/L3 assisted driving | Matching Maextro/M9 gadgets one-for-one (fridge, projector) unless executed at BMW quality | Overt bling with no taste (grille-size controversy); dropping driving dynamics entirely (the S-Class owns pure comfort) |

## 2. Demand trends

| Market | Trend | Data | Src |
|---|---|---|---|
| **EU** | BEV rising, hybrids dominant | EU 2025: BEV 17.4% (from 13.6%), PHEV 9.4%, HEV 34.5%, petrol+diesel 35.5% (from 45.2%) | [S40] |

| **US** | BEV fell after the federal credit ended (30 Sep 2025) | BEV peaked at 12% in Sep 2025, then under 6% per month. HEV+BEV+PHEV about 22% in 2025. Q3 2026 forecast: about 6% EV | [S44][S45] |
